notes.meaning: Pilgrims heading home from Jerusalem call out to the priests and Levites who work through the night in the temple. These temple servants guarded the holy building, tended the altar fire, and kept the lamps burning. Instead of falling asleep or passing the night in idle talk, they are urged to fill their watch with songs of praise to God.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: In traditional Latin and Catholic Bibles, this psalm is numbered 133 and adds that the servants stand in the temple courts. Early church writers like Augustine saw the night watch as a picture of praising God faithfully during dark seasons of trial and loss.

notes.meaning: Lifting up hands was the standard way God's people stood to pray in Bible times. The workers are told to lift clean, holy hands toward the sanctuary, the inner room where God's presence dwelt. The physical action was meant to show that their hearts and thoughts were truly lifted up to the Lord.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine explained that blessing God by night represents remaining faithful during seasons of sorrow and trial, when praise is much harder than in prosperous times.

notes.meaning: The psalm ends with a blessing spoken in return, echoing the words priests spoke over God's people in the wilderness. The Lord is named as the Maker of heaven and earth to remind believers that His power has no limits. Because He chose to dwell among them on Mount Zion, He shares that boundless power with each of His children in tender, fatherly love.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Augustine taught that God addresses 'you' in the singular because He unites all the many individual worshippers into one single body.
